items.title: Canadian Extradited Over University Cryptomining Hacking Scheme Ryan James Roach, 35, of Saskatchewan was extradited to the US on October 28 over a scheme…
items.one_liner: A Canadian hacker was extradited to the U.S. for breaking into university supercomputers to run clandestine cryptomining operations.
items.summary: Ryan James Roach, a 35-year-old Canadian national, was extradited from Saskatchewan to the United States to face charges over an extensive university hacking scheme. Alongside co-defendant Mathiew James Stubbings, Roach allegedly breached the networks of at least four major U.S. universities between mid-2016 and late 2019 to steal credentials and install cryptomining rootkits. The conspirators used fake identities to rent virtual private servers and commandeer supercomputer processing power for illicit cryptocurrency generation. If convicted on the unsealed indictment charges, both men face up to 10 years in federal prison and financial restitution.
key_facts: Maximum Penalty: 10 years in prison, $250,000 fine
items.bottom_line: Cross-border law enforcement cooperation continues to pursue international hackers who compromise academic supercomputing infrastructure for financial gain.

The operation utilizes AI-assisted phishing lures disguised as document-sharing pages hosted on Cloudflare Workers, deceiving victims into running manual commands via a ClickFix trick using PowerShell, mshta, or MSI installers. Once executed, the malicious MSI package installs a private Python runtime and sets up scheduled tasks that communicate via DNS-over-HTTPS beacons to evade standard network monitoring. items.title: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security
items.one_liner: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer goes offline after an unauthorized intrusion compromises user credentials and web dashboards.
items.summary: The RIKEN Center for Computational Science has taken the Fugaku supercomputer offline after discovering unauthorized access to an operational web dashboard between November 10 and 13. Attackers leveraged the dashboard compromise to move across the RIKEN network, install malware on user data servers, and access credentials belonging to 4,222 registered users of Fugaku and 375 users of the Rikyu supercomputer. The intruders subsequently attempted unauthorized login attempts on Fugaku before the machine was shut down. While no research data leakage has been confirmed yet, the outage disrupts ongoing scientific projects as Japanese research facilities face a surge in significant cyber intrusions.
items.bottom_line: A web dashboard compromise led to unauthorized access and credential exposure for thousands of users on Japan's Fugaku supercomputer.
